headline: Qiddiya Awards SAR 5.25bn Performing Arts Centre Contract to Nesma & Partners
deck: The $1.4 billion award covers a three-theatre complex on the Tuwaiq escarpment, the first cultural building at the giga-project to reach construction.
excerpt: Qiddiya Investment Company has awarded a SAR 5.25 billion ($1.4 billion) contract to Nesma & Partners to build the Qiddiya City Performing Arts Centre, a three-theatre complex designed by Tom Wiscombe Architecture. It is the first cultural building at the PIF-owned giga-project to move into construction, and no completion date has been set out.
content:
Qiddiya Investment Company has awarded a SAR 5.25 billion ($1.4 billion) construction contract to the Saudi contractor Nesma & Partners to build the Qiddiya City Performing Arts Centre, the first cultural building at the entertainment giga-project west of Riyadh to move into construction.

The centre will hold three theatres with more than 3,000 seats between them, among them a 500-seat suspended theatre and a cantilevered amphitheatre that projects out over the lower plateau of the site. It has been designed by Tom Wiscombe Architecture, with Brewer Smith Brewer Gulf as design consultant, and Qiddiya expects it to stage more than 200 performances a year once it opens — theatre, music, digital art and touring international productions.

The award is among the largest Qiddiya has placed on a single building, and it is a different kind of contract from the ones that have dominated the project's procurement to date. Qiddiya's earlier packages have been infrastructure, enabling works and themed attractions, including the SAR 3.75 billion contract to build Six Flags Qiddiya City. A performing arts venue sits at the difficult end of the building spectrum.

Most of the cost in a theatre complex is not in the envelope. It is in long-span structure that keeps columns out of sightlines, in acoustic isolation that separates one auditorium from the next and from the ground, in stage machinery, and in the fit-out tolerances that acoustics impose on every surface. Suspending a 500-seat auditorium and cantilevering an amphitheatre over a cliff edge adds transfer structures and deflection control on top of that. Those are the elements that decide whether a building of this type is delivered on its original budget, and they are typically the last to be fully priced.

Nesma & Partners is one of the larger Saudi general contractors and has been active across the Public Investment Fund's project programme. Qiddiya has not published a completion date for the centre, and no phasing for the surrounding cultural district has been set out alongside the award.

Qiddiya City is a PIF-owned development on and below the Tuwaiq escarpment, planned around sport, entertainment and cultural venues rather than housing or offices. The programme's logic is that the anchor assets have to exist before the visitor economy does, which is why the sequencing of large single-purpose buildings matters more here than it would on a mixed-use site where residential sales can be brought forward.

The award also lands in a Saudi contracting market that is absorbing an unusual number of complex vertical packages at once. Riyadh alone has arenas, museums, an opera house and stadium work in procurement or construction, all drawing on the same pool of specialist subcontractors for structural steel, facades, acoustics and theatre engineering — trades that are thin in the region and largely imported. Contract value is the visible number; subcontractor availability is the one that usually sets the programme.

What the award establishes is that Qiddiya has moved past site preparation on its cultural assets and has a main contractor carrying the risk on the hardest one. What it does not establish is a delivery date, and on venues of this type the gap between award and opening is normally measured in years rather than seasons.
author: Mo Qureshi
